title: Account balance cache in a ledger service
name: Ledger balance cache

locateQuestion.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code keeps cached balances consistent with the database? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
locateQuestion.explanation: In transfer(), the cache keys are deleted before COMMIT. Between the delete and the commit, a concurrent getBalance() misses the cache, reads the still-committed old row (READ COMMITTED cannot see the uncommitted update), and writes that old balance back into Redis with a 300 second TTL. After the commit nothing invalidates again, so customers and downstream checks see the pre-transfer balance for up to five minutes. Invalidation must happen after COMMIT succeeds (and ideally use a version check on set).

choiceQuestions.prompt: Two transfers run concurrently: A->B and B->A. What prevents them from deadlocking on the row locks?
choices: The ROLLBACK in the catch block releases locks when Postgres detects the deadlock
Both transactions lock the two rows in sorted account_id order via the SELECT ... ORDER BY ... FOR UPDATE
The conditional UPDATE with available_cents >= $2 never waits on a lock
Each transfer uses its own pooled client, so the locks are independent
choiceQuestions.explanation: The ids are sorted and the SELECT ... ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE acquires both locks in the same global order, so no cycle can form. A rollback after a detected deadlock is recovery, not prevention; the UPDATE does wait on locks; separate clients are exactly what make lock conflicts possible.

choiceQuestions.prompt: If Redis is unreachable while getBalance() runs, what happens?
choices: get() returns null, the balance is read from Postgres, then set() throws and getBalance() rejects
getBalance() returns null as if the account did not exist
The balance is read from Postgres and returned normally because both cache calls swallow errors
getBalance() hangs until the 300 second TTL elapses
choiceQuestions.explanation: BalanceCache.get() catches errors and returns null, so the code falls through to the database. But set() has no try/catch, so its rejection propagates out of getBalance() even though a valid balance was loaded. It does not return null for the account, set() does not swallow errors, and the TTL is unrelated to connection failures.

choiceQuestions.prompt: What does the version column contribute in this code as written?
choices: It is used by set() to refuse overwriting a newer cached balance
It makes the debit UPDATE an optimistic-concurrency check
It is incremented and stored in the cache but nothing compares it, so it does not affect which value wins in Redis
It is used by getBalance() to detect and discard expired cache entries
choiceQuestions.explanation: Both UPDATEs bump version and getBalance() copies it into the cached object, but BalanceCache.set() writes unconditionally and no query filters on version. Concurrency is handled by FOR UPDATE row locks, and expiry is handled only by the Redis TTL.
